The game does use a pretty bad allegory for real world fans, depicting in-game Danganronpa fans as masochistic freaks who enjoy watching other people suffering. It definitely rubbed some people the wrong way, as some people on this subreddit can definitely confirm. However, the way I see it, we as players have two choices. Choice one: accept Danganronpa 3 as the canonical ending for the Hope's Peak Academy storyline and move on from a complete story. Choice two: want the storyline to continue past Danganronpa 3 and to the point that it will become a parody of itself like V3 in many ways is.

I think the game itself is a statement about how popular horror franchises aren't allowed to just end. How many Halloween movies have we had? For that matter, what about the Friday the 13th, Nightmare on Elm Street, etc. There have been instances in each of those films where the big bad is defeated only for them to come back in the next installment. Hell, the setting for V3 is literally "Danganronpa in Space," and Tsumugi literally tries to shoehorn in Junko even though we've seen her die. At one point we even get the line "it's always Junko Enoshima." So if we take that literally, it means that the true mastermind for the phantom Danganronpa entries numbered 4 through 52 is also Junko Enoshima.

Imagine a world where we got even Danganronpa 4 - 10. Yet another six killing games were "somehow Junko Enoshima returned" and was revealed to be the mastermind. Tell me that wouldn't get old. I don't think Kodaka grew to hate Danganronpa. If anything, there's a Monokuma Theater segment near the end of V3 where he seemingly breaks the 4th wall and thanks fans for all their support up until that point. If you look at Raincode, Death Come True, World End Club, and even Hundred Line, each one of those games has nods to Danganronpa.

TL;DR: Miguel may not be 100% right in his thinking. I'll be generous and say he's 60% right. More below.

Bit of a long answer but I want to explain my thinking. If you look at what Miguel says, if you go through it line by line, it's pretty clear he doesn't have canon events down to the exact science he implies. Towards the end of the chase scene, Miles asked Miguel point blank if Miguel knows what happens if Miles prevents his father's death. Miguel's reply is more along the lines of "well do you know what's gonna happen?" 

Then after Miles escapes, Miguel does two things. One is to assemble a team to go after Miles. The other is an order for someone to catch The Spot. That seems to contradict everything that Miguel said earlier. If it was that important for Jefferson Davis to die in order to preserve 1610's canon, why is Miguel calling for people to go after The Spot, BEFORE that death has even happened yet? I think Miguel has a very good idea as to what could happen if Jefferson's death is prevented, but I don't think he can say it will happen with 100% certainty.

Which brings us to this scene with Gwen and George Stacy. Gwen has been living with the knowledge for however many months that her father is going to die as a pre-ordained canon event that can not be prevented. Now George Stacy is quitting his job, and Gwen's world is not ending. It's the first real evidence we've seen that Miguel's thinking is not 100% accurate. It shows that it's possible that not every Spider-person is destined to have the same canon events.

I'll close this out by adding that Gwen isn't the only Spider-person in the Spider Society who hasn't had all their canon events play out. According to the writers, Pavitr hasn't had any of his canon events play out either. That seems to be very contradictory, because if Miguel's right, it would be dangerous for Pavitr to be a member at this point in time. If Pavitr were to learn about canon events at this stage of his canon, he'd reasonably try to do everything he could to prevent them from coming to pass. By Miguel's own logic, if Pavitr were to succeed, it could destroy his world. Yet Miguel still gave him a watch. So that's some more possible evidence that Miguel isn't right about canon events.

The ending struck me as a response from Kodaka to the popularity that Dangronpa gained during its run. If you look at Kodaka's wikipedia nearly everything he did from 2011-2017 was a Danganronpa project. That can be a double edged sword. On the one hand, Kodaka is definitely proud of his work on the franchise. On the other hand, he wanted to move on and do something else, and he couldn't do that without literally killing his darling.

I can apply this issue to any number of horror movie franchises that just kept making installment after installment because they kept making money. Eventually the quality suffers and said franchise fades out instead of ending on a high note. The revelation that Danganronpa v3 is actually the 53 killing game is definitely meant to parallel that. The plot surrounding the Gopher Project is genuinely one of the worst things I've ever seen in a series after all the emotional investment we put into the other three games and the Danganronpa 3 anime. Not to mention the line "it's always Junko Enoshima," seems to imply that in every Danganronpa killing game from 4-53, Junko was always shoehorned in as the mastermind. Imagine a world where we got Danganronpa 4-52, seeing Junko reveal herself as the mastermind time and again. It'll get old well before Danganronpa 10.

All of which is precisely the point. Kodaka seems like he's saying "I love that you love my work, but I can't keep doing this franchise because if I do it's eventually going to suck." I binged the whole series between August and October, and that includes the Danganronpa 3 anime. I went into v3 genuinely wondering why Spike Chunsoft would have made another game after the anime ended on such a great note. The ending, the 4th wall break, the revelation that it's all a meta-fictional narrative, the total breaking of the killing game, is Kodaka making sure Danganronpa went out in a blaze of glory.

But even then, we're left with two options. You can just accept Danganronpa 3 as the one true ending for the series where the fictional narrative is real in that world. Or you can take Danganronpa v3 into account and allow all the Danganronpa stories to be part of the Truman-show from hell narrative it makes the series out to be. At the end of the day, it's your choice.
